chapters.title: Chapter 9: Capstone: Running a Market Making Book Through a Volatile Month

lessons.title: Setting Up the Book: Instrument, Capital, and Risk Limits

body.text: Every decision made before the first quote is even posted, which instrument, how much capital, what limits, already determines how the entire month is going to go. This capstone follows one desk through exactly those decisions, and then through the month that tests them.

children.text: Choosing the Instrument: Bank Nifty Weekly Options

A small desk preparing to run its own market making book for a month chooses Bank Nifty weekly options as its instrument, for reasons that follow directly from Chapter 2. It is liquid enough to have genuine, competitive two-way order flow, without needing an LES appointment from Chapter 1 just to get a two-sided market going at all. It is also volatile and eventful enough, rate-sensitive and reactive to RBI policy days among other things, to plausibly test the desk's full toolkit within a single month, rather than sitting undisturbed the entire time.
Allocating Capital: How Much Is Actually at Risk

The desk sets aside ₹50 lakh as margin capital, the amount needed to hold positions per exchange requirements, but this is not the same as how much it is actually willing to lose. Separately, it sets a hard risk limit: if cumulative losses for the month reach ₹5 lakh, the book pauses entirely for a manual review before resuming, regardless of how much margin capital remains technically available. This distinction, between capital needed to operate and capital the desk is willing to lose before stopping to ask why, is deliberate and foundational, not an afterthought added once trading is already underway.
Setting Position and Risk Limits Using This Course's Own Tools

Rather than picking an inventory limit arbitrarily, the desk works backward from Chapter 6's Little's Law. Given this contract's typical throughput of around 1,200 units per hour, a maximum inventory limit of 300 units implies an average holding time of 300 ÷ 1,200 = 0.25 hours, 15 minutes, which the desk judges an acceptable amount of time to sit exposed to price risk under normal conditions. On top of this, it sets a kill switch, from Chapter 5, that halts all order entry the instant single-session losses exceed ₹1.5 lakh, and the month-level ₹5 lakh drawdown pause from the previous section sits above both of these as a final backstop.

body.caption: The desk's setup for the month

cells: Liquid enough for genuine two-way flow, volatile enough to test the full toolkit
Capital needed to hold positions per exchange requirements
Implies a 15-minute average holding time via Little's Law at typical throughput
Halts all order entry instantly if a session goes badly wrong
Forces a manual review before the book can continue, regardless of remaining margin

body.text: Every one of these numbers traces back to a specific tool from earlier in this course rather than being picked out of thin air: Little's Law for the inventory limit, Chapter 5's kill switch requirement for the single-session trigger, and Chapter 6's emphasis on drawdown, not just P&L, for the month-level pause. This is what it looks like to actually use the material rather than simply having read it.

body.title: Testing an Alternative Inventory Limit
body.prompt: Suppose the desk had instead chosen a maximum inventory limit of 500 units, at the same typical throughput of 1,200 units per hour. Using Little's Law, what average holding time would this imply, in minutes?
body.explanation: W = L ÷ λ = 500 ÷ 1,200 = 0.4167 hours ≈ 25 minutes. A larger inventory limit at the same throughput directly implies a longer average holding time, which is exactly why the desk chose the smaller 300-unit limit instead: it wanted to keep typical exposure time closer to 15 minutes than 25.

body.title: Which Limit Triggers First?
body.scenario: Three weeks into the month, the desk has accumulated ₹3.8 lakh in cumulative losses so far. On this particular session, it is having an unusually bad day and has just lost ₹1.6 lakh intraday, its worst single session yet.
body.prompt: Using the limits set up in this lesson, what happens right now, and what would need to be true for the separate month-level pause to also be triggered?
body.modelAnswer: The kill switch triggers immediately, since the single-session loss of ₹1.6 lakh has just crossed the ₹1.5 lakh threshold, halting all order entry for the rest of this session regardless of the month-to-date total. The month-level ₹5 lakh drawdown pause is a separate, cumulative limit: with ₹3.8 lakh already accumulated before today, this session's loss brings the running total to ₹5.4 lakh, which would also cross the ₹5 lakh threshold and trigger the full monthly pause for manual review, not just today's kill switch.

body.title: Why Two Different Loss Limits Exist
body.question: Why does the desk set both a single-session kill switch and a separate cumulative month-level drawdown pause, rather than relying on just one of them?
options: They are actually the same limit expressed two different ways
The kill switch catches a single catastrophically bad session immediately, while the cumulative limit catches a slower accumulation of smaller losses that no single session would trigger on its own
SEBI requires exactly two loss limits by law, regardless of the desk's own risk appetite
One limit is for equity instruments and the other is only for currency instruments
body.explanation: A single bad session and a slow accumulation of many smaller losses are different failure modes, and a single limit cannot catch both well. The kill switch is built to react fast to an acute single-session problem, exactly as covered in Chapter 5, while the cumulative drawdown pause exists specifically to catch the case where no individual session looks alarming but the trend across many sessions does, which is exactly the situation in this lesson's scenario exercise.

points: This capstone follows one desk's Bank Nifty weekly options book through a full month, chosen specifically for being liquid enough to trade freely and volatile enough to test the full course's toolkit
Margin capital, the amount needed to hold positions, is deliberately kept distinct from a separate, smaller risk limit representing how much the desk is actually willing to lose before pausing
The desk's inventory limit was set by working backward from a target holding time using Little's Law, not chosen arbitrarily
A single-session kill switch and a cumulative month-level drawdown pause serve different purposes, catching an acute single bad day and a slow accumulation of losses respectively
Every parameter in this setup traces back to a specific tool from earlier chapters, which is the entire point of a capstone built this way
